title: India's Rs 1.64 Lakh Crore Chip Bet Now Has 12 Projects — and Its First Production Lines
excerpt: Twelve approved semiconductor projects span six states, Gujarat holds the largest share, and Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi have started commercial production under Semicon 2.0's Rs 1.275 lakh crore outlay.
body:
• India has approved 12 semiconductor projects across six states with committed investment of more than Rs 1.64 lakh crore, according to a government factsheet released ahead of SEMICON India 2026.
  • The projects cover one silicon fab, one silicon carbide fab, an integrated gallium nitride micro-LED display fab and nine packaging units; three facilities — Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi — have started commercial production.
  • Semicon 2.0, approved in July 2026 with an outlay of Rs 1,27,500 crore, extends support across six pillars: design, equipment and materials, fabrication, advanced packaging, R&D and talent.
  • Concentration is the open question: nearly four-fifths of the committed investment sits in Gujarat, per Telecom Live's analysis of the project map.

India's semiconductor programme has crossed the line from announcements to output. A government factsheet released ahead of SEMICON India 2026 counts 12 approved projects across six states with investment commitments of more than Rs 1.64 lakh crore, and three of the approved facilities have already started commercial production, according to Education Post's report of the factsheet. The Financial Express framed the same push as a market story — from chip design to chemicals — and the underlying map explains why.

The map: Gujarat first, then a deliberate spread

Gujarat hosts six of the twelve projects. The flagship is the Tata-PSMC fabrication plant at Dholera, at Rs 91,526 crore with planned capacity above 50,000 wafers a month, followed by Micron Technology's DRAM and NAND assembly and test unit at Sanand (Rs 22,516 crore) and the CG Power–Renesas–Stars OSAT facility (Rs 7,584 crore), with Kaynes Semicon, Crystal Matrix and Suchi Semicon covering packaging, compound semiconductors and discrete devices, as Nation Press detailed from the project list highlighted by former NITI Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant on October 19. Beyond Gujarat: Tata's Rs 27,120 crore OSAT and packaging plant in Assam, SiCSem's silicon carbide facility (Rs 2,066 crore) and 3D Glass Solutions' advanced packaging project (Rs 1,943 crore) in Odisha, and an advanced system-in-package facility in Andhra Pradesh at about Rs 480 crore.

The mix matters. Of the twelve, the approvals include one silicon fab, one silicon carbide fab, an integrated gallium nitride micro-LED display fab and nine packaging units, serving sectors from consumer appliances and automobiles to telecom and aerospace. Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi have started commercial production, with one more unit expected to start in 2026.

Semicon 2.0 widens the funnel

The original Semicon India programme, launched in 2021, carried an outlay of Rs 76,000 crore. Semicon 2.0, approved by the Union Cabinet in July 2026 at Rs 1,27,500 crore, widens support to the supply chain around the fabs: its six pillars are chip design, semiconductor equipment and materials — including the minerals, chemicals and gases fabs consume — fabrication, advanced packaging, research and development, and talent. On the design side, 24 projects from startups and MSMEs have been approved for financial support and 105 startups and MSMEs have access to industry-standard EDA tools under the Design Linked Incentive scheme. The government is targeting 85,000 skilled semiconductor engineers over the decade, with EDA tools deployed across 320 academic institutions and more than 68,000 students trained under the Chips to Startup programme.

What to watch

Two tests will decide whether this becomes an industry or stays a construction story. The first is breadth: Telecom Live calculated that nearly four-fifths of the Rs 1.64 lakh crore is concentrated in Gujarat, with Assam, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh adding different capabilities. The second is the ancillary ecosystem — the equipment, specialty chemicals and gases suppliers Semicon 2.0 now explicitly incentivises. That ecosystem, much of it listed, is where the programme's benefits reach public-market investors first.
